title: 8 haunted places in Iowa, from the Villisca Axe Murder House to the Black Angel
excerpt: From the house of an unsolved murder to a cemetery angel surrounded by spooky legends, these haunted places in Iowa offer a mix of eerie history and local lore.
content:
Like most states, Iowa has a supernatural side, as evidenced by the number of places with stories that are hard to explain away.

Some are tied to real crimes or difficult chapters of history. Others have attracted tales of ghostly visitors, strange sounds, and unexplained happenings. 

If you’re in the mood for spooky stories or paranormal activity, check out these haunted places in Iowa that warrant a deeper look. 

Location: 508 E. 2nd St., Villisca

Let’s start with the obvious—likely Iowa’s most famous spooky tale. 

In the early hours of June 10, 1912, six members of the Moore family and two young guests were killed in their home in Villisca. The brutal murders shocked the small southwestern Iowa community, and despite an extensive investigation and multiple suspects, the case remains unsolved.

More than a century later, the house still stands. Restored to resemble its appearance around the time of the murders, it is now open for historical tours and overnight stays for those interested in its dark history.

The home’s reputation for paranormal activity developed alongside its notoriety. Visitors have reported unexplained sounds, cold spots, and experiences they interpret as encounters with spirits. Some paranormal investigators have also attempted to record electronic voice phenomena, or EVPs, which they believe may capture voices not otherwise audible.

Even without the ghost stories, the house offers a sobering look at a tragedy that remains one of the state’s most enduring mysteries.

Edinburgh Manor

Location: 13241 E23 County Home Rd, Monticello

In rural Jones County, Edinburgh Manor originally served as a county poor farm, providing shelter and food in exchange for labor. The institution later became a home for people who were poor, elderly, or living with mental illness and disabilities. The manor building dates to the early 20th century, and the institution continued operating until 2010.

That long history has helped fuel the stories surrounding the property. Visitors and paranormal investigators have reported hearing voices, encountering shadowy figures, and experiencing other unexplained phenomena. Some accounts describe apparitions of a woman in white and a young girl.

Edinburgh Manor has also attracted attention in online paranormal communities. Visitors who have shared their experiences on Reddit describe returning for investigations, discussing recordings they believe capture voices and swapping stories about the building’s unsettling atmosphere. 

The building’s history is worth exploring alongside the ghost stories. Its former residents lived through difficult circumstances, and their experiences deserve more than a spooky footnote.

Franklin Hotel

Location: 102 Elkader St, Strawberry Point

Strawberry Point’s historic Franklin Hotel dates to the early 1900s. Today, stories about two supposed supernatural residents have become part of its identity.

One is Lily, a woman said to have been a sex worker during the 1920s. Guests have reportedly heard a woman singing or seen an apparition in a gown wandering through the hotel. Room #7 has especially been tied to Lily, with folks saying it is her room or where she spends a lot of time. 

Another figure, Leo, was a longtime resident who ran a laundry business. He had a bell system installed to ring the front desk, and staff say it still rings at night. Guests have also reported furniture moving and other unusual occurrences.

As of late 2025, the hotel has been closed, so for now, you’ll have to live through the online stories. 

Malvern Manor

Location: 103 East 3rd St., Malvern

Malvern Manor has served several purposes since it was built in the late 1800s, including as a hotel and a residential care facility. Today, the building in southwestern Iowa is known largely for its paranormal reputation.

Visitors have reported seeing shadowy figures and hearing voices, footsteps, moans, and screams. Some describe the atmosphere as unsettling even when nothing unusual appears to be happening.

The building’s changing uses give it a history beyond its ghost stories. Like many older institutions, it has seen generations of people pass through its doors, and the stories around it have grown over time.

Cresco Theatre and Opera House

Location: 115 2nd Ave W, Cresco

Not every supposedly haunted Iowa destination is an abandoned building or an old home. In Cresco, a historic theater still welcomes audiences—and, according to local stories, may have a few extra spectators.

The Cresco Theatre and Opera House opened in 1915 as an opera hall before embracing the movie business. It continues to host films, live performances, and community events, making it a working piece of local history rather than a relic of the past.

Theatergoers have described seeing figures that resemble performers onstage or a lone person sitting in the darkened auditorium who seems to disappear when approached. Other stories involve unexplained sounds and electrical disturbances in the building.

You can experience the theater’s real-life history for yourself by catching a movie or performance. Check the Cresco Theatre and Opera House website for the current schedule.

Squirrel Cage Jail

Location: 226 Pearl Street, Council Bluffs

Built in 1885, the Squirrel Cage Jail in Council Bluffs was designed around a rotating cylindrical cell block. Rather than having a traditional corridor lined with individual cells, the jail used a revolving mechanism that allowed the jailer to turn the cell block to control access. The idea was to limit direct contact between jailers and prisoners.

The design was certainly distinctive, but it wasn’t without problems. The mechanism could jam, and the jail eventually closed in 1969.

Today, the building operates as a museum where visitors can see the unusual cell arrangement and learn about the region’s incarceration history. The structure is one of only a few surviving rotary jails and the only known three-story example of its type.

It also has a paranormal reputation. Visitors and museum staff have reported hearing footsteps, voices, and whispers, along with unexplained movement in the building. Stories about deaths associated with the jail add to its unsettling atmosphere.

The Black Angel

Location: 623 N 2nd St, Council Bluffs

In Council Bluffs, a bronze angel standing near Fairview Cemetery has inspired generations of rumors and ghost stories.

Known as the Black Angel, the monument commemorates Ruth Anne Dodge, wife of railroad executive General Grenville Dodge. Before her death in 1916, Ruth Anne reportedly described a recurring dream in which an angel approached her in a boat and offered her water. Her daughters commissioned sculptor Daniel Chester French, who also created the seated Abraham Lincoln at the Lincoln Memorial, to design a monument inspired by the vision.

The resulting sculpture depicts a winged angel standing at the prow of a boat, holding a vessel. Over time, the bronze darkened, giving the statue the black appearance that helped inspire its nickname and ominous reputation.

The folklore surrounding the monument has grown well beyond its origins. Some stories warn that touching her outstretched hand brings death, while others claim she leaves her pedestal at night to fly over Council Bluffs.

Farrar Elementary

Location: 11125 NE 134th Ave, Maxwell, IA 50161

Farrar Elementary, located in a small Polk County community, served local students for generations before closing in 2001. The building later gained a reputation for paranormal activity, with visitors reporting unexplained voices, shadowy figures, and strange sounds throughout the old classrooms and hallways.

Paranormal enthusiasts have visited the property to conduct investigations and share their experiences. Today, visitors can book a tour with paranormal experts to roam the hallways themselves and see what awaits them.
